title: Special assessment, loan or line of credit? What each could cost a Florida condo owner, with the math
seoTitle: Florida Condo Special Assessment vs. Loan: The Real Cost
description: A worked example for Florida condo owners: what a $10,000 share costs as a special assessment, a 5-year loan or a 10-year loan, plus the vote the law requires.
dek: Your board says the repair bill can be paid three ways. They all pay for the same work. What changes is when the money leaves your account, and how much of it goes to interest. Here is a simple example, worked out step by step.
facebook: Pay $10,000 now, or about $121 a month for 10 years? Those are the same repair bill, and one of them costs about $4,559 more. Here's how special assessments, loans and lines of credit compare for a Florida condo owner, with the math done for you.

body.text: When a big repair comes due, a Florida condo board usually has three ways to raise the money: a special assessment, a loan or a line of credit. On paper they look very different. In your checkbook, they all pay for the same work. The differences are timing and interest.

This article walks through one made-up example so you can see the math. Your building's numbers will be different. It is a guide, not legal or financial advice. For your building, the association attorney, the association's accountant and the lender are the people to ask.

body.title: Terms to know
body.text: Special assessment: a one-time charge to every owner on top of regular assessments. It can be due all at once or in installments. Loan: the association borrows a set amount from a lender and pays it back, with interest, over a set number of years. Owners repay it through their assessments. Line of credit: a borrowing limit the association can draw on as needed. Interest is charged on what has been drawn. Majority of the total voting interests: more than half of all the votes in the association, counting owners who don't show up, not just more than half of those who vote.
What Florida law says about all three

Section 718.112(2)(f) of the Florida Statutes lists the ways to fund the reserves a building's SIRS calls for. SIRS stands for structural integrity reserve study, the study that sets how much to save for the main parts of the building, such as the roof, structure and waterproofing. The law says those reserves "may be funded by regular assessments, special assessments, lines of credit, or loans."

Using a special assessment, a line of credit or a loan for those reserves "requires the approval of a majority vote of the total voting interests of the association." The same section says a loan or line of credit used this way, and its details, must be included in the annual financial statement owners receive and in the disclosures given to people buying a unit. Whether other borrowing needs an owner vote can depend on your declaration and bylaws. Ask the association attorney.

Two more rules apply to special assessments. Under section 718.116(10), the written notice must state the specific purpose, and the money collected may be used only for that purpose. If money is left over when the work is done, it is treated as common surplus, and the board may refund it or credit it to future assessments. Under section 718.112(2)(c), the notice of a meeting to consider a nonemergency special assessment must reach owners at least 14 days ahead and must state the estimated cost and purpose.

Say a 100-unit building needs $1 million of work, and each unit's share is the same: $10,000. In real buildings, shares usually follow the percentages in the declaration, so larger units often pay more. We also assume an interest rate of 8% a year on any loan. That rate is only for the example. Real rates depend on the lender, the building and the day the loan is signed.

items: Special assessment, paid at once: $10,000. No interest. The hardest month, but the cheapest total.
Special assessment in 12 monthly installments: about $833 a month for a year. Still $10,000 total if the association charges no interest on the installments.
Loan over 5 years at 8%: about $202.76 a month for 60 months. Total about $12,166, so about $2,166 goes to interest.
Loan over 10 years at 8%: about $121.33 a month for 120 months. Total about $14,559, so about $4,559 goes to interest.

body.text: The pattern is the point. A longer loan makes each month smaller and the total bigger. In this example, the 10-year loan costs almost half again as much as paying the $10,000 up front.
Where a line of credit fits

A line of credit works more like a credit card with a limit. The association draws money as the work moves along, and interest is charged on what has been drawn, not on the whole limit. If a project is paid in stages, that can mean less interest early on than a loan taken all at once. Before a vote, owners can ask three plain questions: What is the limit? Can the rate change? When does it have to be paid back?

items: Paying your share early. Some associations let owners pay their portion of a loan up front so they don't carry their share of the interest. A Becker & Poliakoff Q&A column notes this raises legal and procedural questions for the association. Ask whether it is an option, and in writing.
Selling while a loan is open. A loan or line of credit used for SIRS reserves must appear in the disclosures to buyers. A buyer will see it, and the monthly amount may come with the unit.

Falling behind. Under section 718.116(3), unpaid assessments carry interest at the rate in the declaration, or 18% a year if the declaration sets none, and an administrative late fee if the declaration or bylaws allow it. That can turn a missed payment into a much bigger one.
The lender's terms. The same Becker column says most banks require a special assessment as collateral for an association loan. So a loan and a special assessment are often used together.
Find your share. Ask the manager or board what your unit's portion is, in dollars, under each option.
Ask for the total cost, not just the monthly number: rate, term, fees and total repaid.
Ask whether you can pay your share up front, and what happens to the interest if you do.
Check the notice. It should state the purpose and estimated cost. Keep it with your records.
If a payment would be hard, talk to the manager before it is late, not after.
Put the options side by side for owners with per-unit monthly and total cost. A one-page table answers most questions before the meeting.
Ask the association attorney which owner votes the declaration, bylaws and section 718.112(2)(f) require for the option you are considering.
Ask the engineer or reserve professional whether the SIRS must be updated. The law says the study must take the funding method into account.
Ask the accountant how the loan or line of credit will be shown in the annual financial statement.

faq.q: Is a condo special assessment or a loan cheaper?
faq.a: Paying a special assessment at once usually costs the least in total because there is no interest. A loan lowers the monthly amount but adds interest. In our example, a $10,000 share cost about $14,559 over a 10-year loan at 8%.

faq.q: Can my Florida condo board borrow money without an owner vote?
faq.a: Using a special assessment, loan or line of credit to fund the reserves required by the SIRS needs a majority vote of the total voting interests under section 718.112(2)(f). Other borrowing can depend on your declaration and bylaws. The association attorney can tell you which applies.

faq.q: Can I pay my share of the condo association loan up front?
faq.a: Some associations allow it, so owners don't carry their share of the interest. It depends on how the association and lender set it up. Ask the manager or board in writing.

faq.q: Can a condo association use special assessment money for something else?
faq.a: No. Under section 718.116(10), the money may be used only for the purpose stated in the notice. Any money left over is common surplus, which the board may refund or credit to future assessments.

faq.q: What happens if I can't pay a condo special assessment on time?
faq.a: Unpaid assessments carry interest at the rate in the declaration, or 18% a year if none is set, and possibly a late fee, under section 718.116(3). Talk to the association manager before a payment is late.
